implementation_notes: With gRPC the Detour is an interceptor: build the interceptor-factory vector and hand it to ServerBuilder::experimental().SetInterceptorCreators() only while the toggle is on, so the stage applies per RPC to every method of that server and the messages still end up in the same service implementation. Without an interceptor-capable framework the manual form is a std::vector<std::function<void(Order&)>> stage chain assembled at start-up with the detour stage pushed in conditionally - both forms keep one shared delivery call, which is what separates a Detour from a wire tap. Choose the interceptor form when gRPC is already the transport; choose the std::function chain for in-process pipelines and batch flows where the toggle is fixed at start-up.
pitfalls: Interceptor order is the routing contract: pushing the detour in changes the order in which metadata and errors are seen relative to the other interceptors.
Interceptors are per-call, not per-connection: replay buffers, timers or any state that must survive a message has to live outside the interceptor.
Rebuilding the server to flip the flag defeats the purpose - read the toggle per call (or re-register creators deliberately) instead of recompiling.

variants.name: std::function stage chain assembled at start-up
variants.idiom_name: std::vector<std::function<void(Order&)>> with a conditionally inserted stage
variants.implementation_notes: The framework-free form: keep the route as a vector of std::function stages and push the detour stage in only when the configuration enables it; every stage mutates the order in place and the single deliver(order) call at the end is the destination for both legs. Choose it for embedded, batch or in-process pipelines where no interceptor-capable framework is in the stack and the toggle may be fixed at start-up. A runtime flip needs an atomic check inside the stage (or a pointer swap under a lock), because the stage list itself is built once.
variants.code_sketch:
using Stage = std::function<void(Order&)>;

std::vector<Stage> stages{validate_order};               // normal route
if (cfg.detour_enabled) stages.push_back(trace_order);   // detour stage

for (auto& stage : stages) stage(order);                 // inspect/modify in place
deliver(order);                                          // same destination, both legs
pitfalls: Every stage must be side-effect-free with respect to the destination contract, or the detour changes business outcomes instead of adding inspection.
A stage captured by reference in a std::function that outlives the configuration object is the classic dangling-reference bug.
